rationale: The hypothesis posits that all confirmed cases of Jaberi-Elahi syndrome (JES) harbor biallelic truncating, frameshift, or critical splice-site loss-of-function variants driving a strictly homogeneous phenotype. This is directly refuted by recent clinical and molecular reports. Multiple studies identify pathogenic or likely pathogenic missense variants associated with JES (e.g., Manoochehri et al. 2024 reporting c.1289T>C [p.Leu430Pro], Vedula et al. 2026 reporting a novel homozygous missense variant in exon 7, and Soğukpınar et al. 2026 documenting five missense variants among 20 distinct GTPBP2 variants). Furthermore, phenotypic presentation shows notable variability (such as the absence of skeletal findings in specific probands and variable presence of visual impairment [18/28]), demonstrating that the mutational spectrum extends beyond classic truncating loss-of-function mutations and phenotypic presentation is not strictly uniform.

evidence.text: In a literature review of 28 patients with Jaberi-Elahi syndrome, the authors describe a novel homozygous missense variant (NM_019096.5:c.1289T>C, p.Leu430Pro) expanding the genetic spectrum beyond truncating variants. Phenotypic frequencies showed motor developmental delay in 26/28, sparse hair in 26/28, speech disorder in 24/28, intellectual disability in 23/28, hypotonia in 23/28, skeletal abnormalities in 23/28, and visual impairment in 18/28.

source.title: Jaberi-Elahi syndrome: Exploring a novel GTPBP2 mutation and a literature review
source.quote: In summary, we present evidence implicating a novel missense variant in Jaberi-Elahi syndrome, expanding and refining the genetic spectrum of this condition... A large numbers of patients manifest motor development delay (26/28), sparse hair (26/28), and speech disorder (24/28). Moreover, a significant fraction of patients suffer from intellectual disability (23/28), hypotonia (23/28), skeletal problems (23/28), and visual impairment (18/28). In spite of previous patients, the proband in this study did not exhibit any skeletal abnormalities.

evidence.text: A comprehensive review of reported GTPBP2 variants reveals 20 distinct variants across Jaberi-Elahi syndrome patients, comprising nine nonsense variants, five missense variants, and other frameshift alleles, contradicting the assertion that all cases harbor truncating or splice-site loss-of-function variants.

conflicts: The hypothesis asserts that all confirmed cases carry biallelic truncating, frameshift, or splice-site LoF variants, whereas Manoochehri et al. (2024), Soğukpınar et al. (2026), and Vedula et al. (2026) confirm that at least 5 missense variants cause or contribute to the syndrome.

The hypothesis assumes an invariant, homogeneous clinical manifestation, whereas cohort analyses demonstrate incomplete penetrance of key findings, such as visual impairment (18/28) and skeletal abnormalities (absent in the proband described by Manoochehri et al., present in 23/28).

new_directions.question_text: Do missense variants in GTPBP2 produce hypomorphic alleles that result in milder, non-progressive, or atypical neurodevelopmental phenotypes compared to truncating biallelic null alleles?
new_directions.rationale: Given that missense variants have now been documented in multiple cohorts, functional assays comparing ribosomal stalling/rescue efficiency between null and missense alleles will clarify genotype-phenotype correlations.

new_directions.question_text: What imaging and clinical criteria best distinguish Jaberi-Elahi syndrome from Joubert syndrome and related ciliopathies presenting with cerebellar hypoplasia and hypotonia?
new_directions.rationale: D'Abrusco et al. (2022) revealed misdiagnosis of GTPBP2-related disease as Joubert syndrome due to pseudomolar tooth signs on MRI; defining true versus mimicked neuroradiological signs is essential for differential diagnosis.
